971.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
971.explanation: In this salok Guru Arjan ties real life to udham, the effort a person actually puts in. For Sikhs this effort is both honest work (kirat) and the steady practice of the Name, and the Gurus repeatedly reject the idle hope that life will turn out well without it.
971.tie_back: The Kural calls an abundance of inner drive a person's glory and the thought of getting by without it a disgrace, and Guru Arjan likewise makes effort the condition of a life that is really lived.
971.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
971._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Sant Singh Khalsa translation via the BaniDB database behind sikhitothemax.org; a strong fit on effort as what gives life its worth, though Guru Arjan has spiritual effort chiefly in view, where the Kural speaks of worldly zeal.

972.quote_or_event: “First, Allah created the Light; then, by His Creative Power, He made all mortal beings. From the One Light, the entire universe welled up. So who is good, and who is bad?”
972.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, a low-caste weaver whose hymns the Gurus placed in the scripture, says that every person comes from the same divine Light. Birth therefore gives no one superiority, and the Sikh tradition draws from this its rejection of caste.
972.tie_back: Like Valluvar's claim that all are equal at birth, Kabir's verse refuses to rank people by where they come from, which leaves only conduct to tell them apart.
972.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1349, Raag Prabhaati, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
972._accuracy_note: Both lines verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a near match on equality of birth, though the Kural's second half, that distinction comes from deeds, is implied here rather than stated.

973.quote_or_event: “Nanak seeks the company of the lowest of the low class, the very lowest of the low. ... In that place where the lowly are cared for-there, the Blessings of Your Glance of Grace rain down.”
973.explanation: Guru Nanak deliberately takes his place among those society ranks lowest and says God's grace falls where the lowly are cared for. The verse overturns the idea that social position measures a person's worth.
973.tie_back: The Kural says the base are not high even on a high seat and the noble are not low even when placed low, and Guru Nanak gives the same reversal, siding with the people the world calls low.
973.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
973._accuracy_note: Both lines verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa; the ellipsis marks an omitted half-line); a strong thematic fit on rank not equalling worth, though the Guru speaks of choosing the lowly rather than of the low remaining noble.

974.quote_or_event: “You search for your Husband Lord; you must have some fault in your body. Those who are known as happy soul-brides, do not look to others.”
974.explanation: In these saloks the faithful soul-bride (suhagan) is the one whose devotion is undivided and who does not look elsewhere. Gurbani uses this image for the disciplined soul that keeps itself wholly for God.
974.tie_back: Valluvar compares the greatness of the self-guarding person to a woman of single-hearted faithfulness, and the Granth's happy soul-bride who does not look to others is the same image of guarded, undivided loyalty.
974.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 114 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
974._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; the faithful-bride image matches the Kural's simile, but in Gurbani the bride is the soul and the faithfulness is spiritual devotion to God, not marital chastity as the ground of social greatness.

975.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. ... give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
975.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the Sikh path as something only the wholehearted can take up: one must be ready to give one's very head. Sikh tradition later saw this demand fulfilled in the Gurus' and early Sikhs' willingness to face martyrdom.
975.tie_back: The Kural says the truly great accomplish what others find too hard, and Guru Nanak sets exactly such a hard path, open only to those who will give everything.
975.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, salok 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
975._accuracy_note: First, second and fourth lines verified verbatim via BaniDB (the ellipsis omits the third); a reasonable fit on greatness shown in doing the very hard thing, though Guru Nanak speaks of devotion rather than of accomplishing difficult deeds in general.

976.quote_or_event: Macauliffe recounts that when Guru Nanak's end drew near he appointed his devoted disciple Angad (Bhai Lehna), who had served him wholeheartedly, as his successor, because the Guru's own sons had not obeyed him: their minds were insincere and they had rebelled and deserted him.
976.explanation: In the Sikh account Lehna's readiness to serve the Guru and make the Guru's way his own is what made him Guru Angad, while the Guru's sons, though close to him by birth, never sought that service. Britannica likewise notes that Angad was known for his loyalty to the first Guru.
976.tie_back: The Kural says the resolve to cherish the great and take on their way never arises in small minds, and the story sets Lehna, who had that resolve, against the sons, who lacked it.
976.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter XVII; corroborated by Encyclopaedia Britannica, Guru Angad
976._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Macauliffe Vol. 1 ch. XVII on sacred-texts.com, which draws on the Janamsakhi tradition, so the details are hagiographic; it is a strong narrative fit for seeking to serve and become like the great.

977.quote_or_event: “Royal power, wealth, beauty, social status and youth are the five thieves. These thieves have plundered the world; no one’s honor has been spared.”
977.explanation: Guru Nanak lists the very things that raise a person in the world (power, wealth, beauty, status, youth) and calls them thieves. Unless a person is anchored in the Guru, they lead to ruin, and the next line says only those who fall at the Guru's feet rob these robbers.
977.tie_back: The Kural warns that distinction falling to the unworthy turns into excess, and Guru Nanak names the same gifts of eminence as forces that plunder anyone who is not inwardly fit to hold them.
977.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar, Vaar Malaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
977._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong fit, since both texts treat rank, wealth and status as dangerous in unworthy hands, though Guru Nanak is warning everyone, not only the unworthy.

978.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak! Are the essence of virtue and goodness. Everyone bows down to himself; no one bows down to another. When something is placed on the balancing scale and weighed, the side which descends is heavier.”
978.explanation: The salok begins with the simmal tree, tall and showy but with useless fruit, and contrasts it with humility. On a scale the heavier pan sinks lower, so true worth shows itself by bowing.
978.tie_back: Valluvar says greatness always bows while littleness admires and adorns itself, and Guru Nanak's image of the heavier pan sinking makes the same point.
978.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
978._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; near one-to-one, with the bowing of the weighty set against the showy tall tree closely matching the Kural's contrast.

979.quote_or_event: “The humble beings abide in peace; subduing egotism, they are meek. The very proud and arrogant persons, O Nanak! Are consumed by their own pride.”
979.explanation: This salok opens the twelfth ashtapadi of Sukhmani, which goes on to list the pride of power, beauty, wealth and even of good deeds as forms of haumai (ego) that destroy a person. Haumai is the root problem in Sikh teaching.
979.tie_back: The Kural defines greatness as the absence of arrogance and littleness as riding on it, and Guru Arjan likewise contrasts the meek who live in peace with the proud who are consumed by their pride.
979.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Ashtapadi 12 (opening salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
979._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a near match on humility as greatness and pride as ruin.

980.quote_or_event: “Farid, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
980.explanation: Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose saloks the Gurus placed in the scripture, tells the wise not to tally other people's faults but to look at their own. Elsewhere Gurbani condemns nindaa (slander) as a sign of the self-willed.
980.tie_back: The Kural says greatness covers others' weaknesses while littleness speaks only of faults, and Farid gives the same instruction: refuse to blacken others and look inward instead.
980.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
980._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong fit on not dwelling on others' faults, though Farid adds self-examination where the Kural speaks of actively concealing others' weak points.
